newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Booming Ireland to hold election on June 6.
newsitem.headline: Booming Ireland to hold election on June 6.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton on Thursday called a national election for June 6, gambling that the "feelgood factor" from a booming economy would trim the resurgent opposition's 11-point opinion poll lead.

Bruton, whose three-party "Rainbow coalition" came to power in late 1994, had until November to call the election but opted to stage it early in the wake of what he called the biggest tax giveaway budget in the 75 years of the state.

He told parliamentary colleagues from his own Fine Gael party and allies Labour and the Democratic Left that they should fight off the opposition on the coalition's record of creating jobs and prosperity.

"Promises are one thing. Performance is another. Jobs are the centrepiece of this government. We want to halve unemployment and add 1,000 jobs each week over the next five years just as we have over the last two years," he said.

His rival, Bertie Ahern of Fianna Fail, was confident the poll would return a "young, invigorated government into the next millennium". He said there were no policy differences with his likely coalition ally, the Progressive Democrats of Mary Harney.
"We can all be happy. The sun is out this morning and the Rainbow will be out in a few weeks," Harney quipped.

Opinion polls show the popularity of the ruling coalition has been fading fast in the wake of revelations that an Irish tycoon, Ben Dunne, paid millions of pounds to politicians from all parties, including Bruton's Fine Gael.
A Bruton protege, Michael Lowry, resigned as transport minister last year after admitting that Dunne had paid for the renovation of his private home in a complex business deal.

An official inquiry heard that former Fianna Fail prime minister Charles Haughey also received more than a million pounds ($1.6 million) from Dunne to ease cash problems, but the party does not seem to have suffered.

Irish elections are held under a proportional representation system. A poll last week gave Fianna Fail 43 per cent of votes with the Progressive Democrats taking eight. For the coalition, Fine Gael was on 26 percent, Labour 12 and Democratic Left two.
This 51-40 lead almost doubled the six-point advantage the opposition had held over the coalition until the "payments-to-politicians" tribunal began its hearings this month.
Financial markets took the news in their stride. The date had been widely publicised and caused no surprises.
Polls apart, history is against Bruton. For almost 30 years no incumbent Irish government has been returned at the polls.
Unemployment, the management of one of Europe's most successful economies, law and order and the Northern Ireland peace process are expected to dominate the campaign.
Fine Gael says that since it took over in 1994 it has brought the jobless rate down from around 13 percent to 11 and shaved taxes by a percentage point in its budget in January.

But Ahern is expected to make a firm pledge to get the top rate of tax down from 48 per cent to 43 per cent in the next five-year parliament, a vote-winning promise that may sway a nation that complains of one of Europe's heaviest tax burdens.

Both opposition and government parties have promised to crack down on crime, especially drug trafficking, after the unsolved murder last year of Veronica Guerin, Ireland's top investigative reporter, by the drugs underworld.

Both are committed to a peaceful settlement of the Northern Ireland conflict but Ahern says Fianna Fail will be much more assertive in dealing with Britain, Dublin's partner in a slow-moving peace process.
The previous coalition led by Fianna Fail's Albert Reynolds collapsed when its then ally, the Labour party, withdrew its support in November 1994 in a row over legal appointments.
